questions.question: What is GitFlow and what are its main branches?
questions.title: GitFlow Workflow Explained
questions.direct_answer: GitFlow is a branching model with five branch types: main (production), develop (integration), feature/* (new features), release/* (release prep), and hotfix/* (urgent production fixes).

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of structured team workflows — commonly asked in enterprise/product company interviews
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing up which branches merge into which — not knowing that hotfix merges to both main and develop
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that GitFlow is considered heavyweight today and many modern teams prefer GitHub Flow or trunk-based development

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: GitFlow is a branching model popularized by Vincent Driessen that defines a strict set of branch types and how they interact. It has five types of branches. Main (or master) always contains production-ready code — only release and hotfix branches merge into it. Develop is the integration branch where all features come together and is the branching point for new features. Feature branches — named feature/something — branch off develop, contain work for one specific feature, and merge back into develop when done. Release branches — release/1.2.0 — branch off develop when you're ready to prepare a release. You do bug fixes and versioning here, then merge into both main and develop. Hotfix branches — hotfix/critical-bug — branch off main when you need an emergency fix in production. They merge into both main and develop. GitFlow made a lot of sense in the era of scheduled releases every few months. For teams deploying continuously — multiple times a day — it's often considered overkill. Most modern startups use GitHub Flow instead.

sections.title: Key Points
content: main: production code; develop: integration/staging branch
feature/*: branches off develop, merges back into develop
release/*: branches off develop, merges into main AND develop
hotfix/*: branches off main for emergency fixes, merges into main AND develop
GitFlow suits scheduled-release enterprises; GitHub Flow suits continuous deployment teams

questions.question: What is GitHub Flow and how does it differ from GitFlow?
questions.title: GitHub Flow vs GitFlow
questions.direct_answer: GitHub Flow is a simpler workflow: main is always deployable, features are built on short-lived branches, and changes go to main via pull requests — no develop, release, or hotfix branches.

interviewer_intent.testing: Familiarity with modern team workflows — GitHub Flow is what most startups and fast-moving teams use
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that GitHub Flow's simplicity is intentional, not a dumbed-down version of GitFlow
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that GitHub Flow works best with feature flags for hiding incomplete features from users while still shipping to production

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: GitHub Flow is a deliberately simple workflow. The whole model is: main is always deployable, anything on main has been tested and can go to production at any time. When you want to work on something — feature, fix, experiment — you create a descriptively named branch off main. You make commits, push to the remote, and open a pull request early so the team can see and discuss. When the PR is reviewed and approved and CI passes, you merge it into main. Main is then deployed. That's the entire workflow. No develop branch, no release branches, no hotfix branches — just main and short-lived feature branches. It works really well for continuous deployment environments because the simplicity removes overhead. The key assumption is that you can deploy at any time, which requires good CI/CD and potentially feature flags for features that aren't ready to show users even if the code is deployed. GitFlow was designed for teams with scheduled releases every few weeks or months. GitHub Flow is designed for teams shipping multiple times a day.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Two branch types: main (always deployable) + short-lived feature branches
No develop, release, or hotfix branches — significantly simpler than GitFlow
Feature branch → PR → review + CI → merge to main → deploy
Works best with continuous deployment and feature flags
Used by GitHub itself and most modern startups; GitFlow suits enterprises with scheduled releases

questions.question: What is trunk-based development?
questions.title: Trunk-Based Development
questions.direct_answer: Trunk-based development (TBD) is a workflow where all developers integrate small changes directly into a single main branch (trunk) frequently — often multiple times a day — with very short-lived branches of hours to days, not weeks.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of modern DevOps practices — TBD is used by Google, Facebook, and many high-velocity teams
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking TBD means no branches — branches are still used, they're just very short-lived
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that TBD requires feature flags and strong CI to work well — you're merging incomplete features but hiding them

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Trunk-based development is the practice of integrating code changes into the main branch (the 'trunk') very frequently — ideally multiple times a day per developer. The idea is that long-lived branches are the root cause of many integration problems: the longer a branch lives, the more it diverges, the worse the merge conflict, the more bugs hide undiscovered. By merging small changes to trunk constantly, integration is continuous and conflicts are trivial. Feature branches in TBD exist but are measured in hours or 1-2 days maximum, not weeks. The key enabler is feature flags — you can merge code for an incomplete feature into main as long as it's hidden behind a flag. CI becomes even more critical: you need tests that run fast and catch regressions immediately because main is always being updated. Google is famous for practicing extreme TBD across millions of lines of code and thousands of engineers. For freshers, knowing this exists and why it's used — reduced integration pain, faster feedback — is valuable context.

sections.title: Key Points
content: All developers integrate to main (trunk) frequently — multiple times a day
Feature branches are short-lived: hours to 1-2 days maximum
Requires feature flags to ship incomplete features without exposing them to users
Requires strong, fast CI — tests must catch regressions quickly on every merge
Used by Google, Facebook, and Netflix — reduces big-bang integration pain

questions.question: What is a .gitignore file and what should go in it?
questions.title: .gitignore Basics
questions.direct_answer: A .gitignore file tells Git which files and directories to ignore and never track — typically build outputs, IDE files, logs, dependency folders, and files with secrets like .env.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic professionalism — accidentally committing .env secrets or target/ folders is a common junior mistake
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Committing the target/ directory, node_modules/, or .env files — these are the most common gitignore mistakes
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention gitignore.io (a tool to generate .gitignore for your tech stack) and .gitignore templates on GitHub

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A .gitignore file is placed in the root of your repository and contains patterns of files and directories that Git should completely ignore — they won't show up in 'git status' as untracked and 'git add .' won't pick them up. For a Java/Spring Boot project, the typical .gitignore includes: the target/ directory (Maven's build output — these are generated files, not source code), .class files, IDE-specific directories like .idea/ for IntelliJ or .vscode/ for VS Code (different developers use different IDEs, no need to commit these), application.properties files that contain environment-specific secrets or credentials, and any .env files. You should never commit secrets to Git — once something is in the git history, it's very hard to fully remove. For the IDE folders and build directories, generating them on any machine from the source code is trivial. A useful resource: gitignore.io lets you pick your tech stack and generates a comprehensive .gitignore file. GitHub also provides templates when you create a new repository.

sections.title: Key Points
content: .gitignore contains patterns of files Git should not track or show as untracked
Always ignore: target/ (Maven build output), .idea/ / .vscode/ (IDE configs), *.class, *.log
Never commit: .env files, application secrets, credentials — once in git history, hard to purge
Each line is a pattern; '#' is a comment; '!' negates a pattern (re-include an ignored file)
gitignore.io: generate stack-specific .gitignore files automatically

questions.question: What are conventional commits and why do teams use them?
questions.title: Conventional Commits
questions.direct_answer: Conventional Commits is a specification for commit message format using type prefixes like 'feat:', 'fix:', 'docs:' — enabling automated changelog generation, semantic versioning, and better searchability of git history.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of structured team conventions — shows the candidate has experience or interest in professional team tooling
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing conventional commits exist, or thinking the type prefix is just stylistic — it enables automation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that breaking changes are indicated with 'BREAKING CHANGE:' in the footer or '!' after the type — e.g., 'feat!: rename API endpoint'

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Conventional Commits is a specification that standardizes commit message format across a team. The format is: type(scope): description. Common types are 'feat' for new features, 'fix' for bug fixes, 'docs' for documentation, 'refactor' for code refactoring without behavior change, 'test' for adding tests, 'chore' for build tasks or maintenance, and 'perf' for performance improvements. For example: 'feat(auth): add JWT refresh token endpoint', 'fix(user-service): resolve NPE when email is null', 'docs(readme): update setup instructions'. The scope in parentheses is optional but useful for larger codebases. Why do teams use this? First, it makes git log much more readable — you can scan and understand each commit's purpose at a glance. Second, tooling can parse these messages automatically. Tools like semantic-release can read your commits and determine whether a code change warrants a major, minor, or patch version bump, and auto-generate a CHANGELOG. Breaking changes are marked with 'BREAKING CHANGE:' in the footer or '!' after the type: 'feat!: rename /users endpoint to /api/users'.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Format: type(scope): description — e.g., 'feat(auth): add OAuth2 support'
Common types: feat, fix, docs, refactor, test, chore, perf, ci
Enables automated changelog generation and semantic versioning via tools like semantic-release
Breaking changes: 'BREAKING CHANGE:' in footer or '!' after type: 'feat!: rename endpoint'
Standardizes team history — makes git log scannable and searchable by type
